lines.text: Highland imams, an empire builder, a defiant no to France and a long struggle since. This is the story of Guinea.
In the highlands of Fouta Djallon, the Fula people founded a Muslim state ruled by imams, which lasted for nearly two centuries.
Samori Toure built the Wassoulou Empire, and fought the French for sixteen years before he was captured.
On a peninsula in the Atlantic, the French founded Conakry, which became the capital of their colony.
Ahmed Sekou Toure was born, the man who would lead Guinea to independence and rule it for a quarter of a century.
Lansana Conte, a soldier, would take power after him and hold it until his death.
Alpha Conde would become Guinea's first freely elected president, until a coup removed him.
On the border with Ivory Coast, the mountain forests of Mount Nimba were set aside as a strict nature reserve.
Mory Kante would carry the kora and Guinean song to dance floors around the world.
In 1958, Guinea voted no to France, the first French colony in Africa to choose independence. It was free that same year.
But under Toure, thousands of his opponents died in the prison of Camp Boiro.
Mamady Doumbouya was born, the colonel who would seize power in 2021.
In 2013, the largest Ebola outbreak ever known began in Guinea and spread to its neighbours, killing many health workers.
From the highland imams to the vote of 1958, Guinea has always made its own choices.
